titulo: The coins you leave, and the second time you walk in
subtitulo: What a table here actually leaves on the little plate, the four words that hand it over, the one job on this trip where the tip is somebody's wage, and how to let the other hand get there first
cena: Ten past four on a Sunday, three of you at the end of a long lunch, twenty-eight sixty on the little plate, and everybody has gone quiet and is waiting to see what somebody puts on top of it.
decisao: how much goes on top of the bill, and who puts it there — the rounding the next table leaves against the fifth of it your hand wants to leave, across twenty-eight paid meals; and whether the counter you walk back into on Thursday reads you as somebody who lives here this week or as somebody passing through

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you those sentences. You put a coin down and said four words, and you never once did a sum.
clique.piso: You will leave what the next table leaves, without a single sum. Most visitors pay a fifth more all fortnight and never find out.

frasePiso: You will leave what the next table leaves, without a single sum. Most visitors pay a fifth more all fortnight and never find out.
permissao: Round it up. That is the whole system, and nothing at all is an ordinary amount to leave — the tip here is extra, not the wage, and nobody goes home short because of you. You are allowed to put your wallet away when somebody's hand stops yours, and you are allowed to hand over notes and say four words without working out a single percentage.
espelho: Working out a percentage at the table is the bit that reads as odd there. Nobody at that table is doing sums, and the one who is doing sums is the one being watched.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The notes go down on the little plate, the coins out of the change stay where they are, and nobody at the table counts them or mentions them.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That is almost nothing. I should put more down, or the person who has been looking after us all afternoon is out of pocket because of me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Waiting staff here are on a salary and a collective agreement, so what stays on the plate is a rounding rather than an income. A table that rounds up has done the ordinary thing, and a table that leaves nothing has also done the ordinary thing.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Round the total up to something tidy, leave it, and stand up. No sum, no announcement, no apology.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You leave what the next table leaves, and the money your hand wanted to give away out of habit buys the last night of the holiday instead.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not the walk that was sold to you as free. There what goes into the guide's hand at the end is the wage, and that one you pay properly.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You reach for your wallet, a hand comes across and stops yours, and the other person has already given the man a note.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He has just paid for me and I barely know him. I have to get my money out or I look like somebody taking advantage.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: One person settles the whole thing and the next one comes round to you — the going round is the point of it, and the wrestling match over the plate is the part that turns money into a scene.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Let it go, put your wallet away, thank him, and put a name on the next one out loud.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: There is a next one, which is the entire reason he did it, and you are the one who gets there first the following morning.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not with somebody you have just met and will not see again, and not on a bill big enough to hurt — there you say the separate one from part fourteen, before he closes anything.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The walk finishes in a square, the guide says thank you and takes a step back, and nobody has been asked for anything at all.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: It said free on the website, so it was free, and everybody drifting off is what is supposed to happen.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: On a walk advertised as free, what goes into that hand at the end is what the guide is paid — it is the one job you will meet on this trip with a real expectation attached to it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Have notes in your pocket before it ends, go up to her, put it in her hand and say thank you to her face.

steps.pt: Part twenty-eight. Warm-up: the flick. One tap of the tongue, never a roll. Gra-cias. Pro-pi-na. Ver-dad.
Finger flicks once and stops. If it buzzes, you have rolled it. Three more, out loud, on your leg.

steps.promptPt: Three of you, one bill, and nobody wants to sit there working out who had the extra beer. Tell him how to do it. Speak now.
steps.pt: one total, split down the middle
Ten past four on a Sunday. Three of you, a long lunch, and the little plate with the paper on it has landed.
Twenty-eight sixty. Everybody has gone quiet, and a hand is already reaching for a phone to work something out.
Nobody at the next table is doing that. What they do instead takes four words, and we get to them shortly.
First, one question he asks on his way over. It has two answers, and you have owned one of them since part fourteen.

steps.pinyin: bah TOH-dhoh KHOON-toh oh por seh-pah-RAH-dhoh
steps.pt: 👂 'All on one, or separately?' — asked before he rings anything up, not after.
The other answer is two words, and it means the evening is yours. It is the one you will hear yourself using.
All on one, please.

steps.promptPt: Four of you on the terrace, the plates are gone, and he is coming over asking how he should ring it up. Tonight is on you. Speak now.
steps.pt: one bill, and it is yours
👂 'Card or cash?' — decide before he walks back with the machine.
Right. What actually gets left, place by place. Coffee at the counter: nothing, or the coins out of your change.
Neighbourhood bar, the set lunch: round it up. Fifty cents. A euro. Nobody is counting and nobody minds.
A proper evening you genuinely loved: five to ten per cent. Most tables here leave less than that, or nothing.
Taxi: round it up. The man who carries your cases up three floors: a euro or two, in cash, in his hand.
One job on this trip sits outside that whole table, and it is the last thing we do today. Hold on to that.
Now the line that resets an English-speaking head. Waiting staff here are on a salary and a collective agreement.
The tip is extra. It is not the income. Leaving nothing harms nobody, and nobody goes home short because of you.
The sums, quickly, because they are funnier than they are important. A set lunch averages fourteen euros twenty.
A twenty per cent reflex on that is two eighty-four. Rounding it up to fifteen is eighty cents. Two euros a meal.
Twice a day, a fortnight, two of you: about a hundred and fifteen euros. And the money is not the interesting bit.
Nobody was expecting anything, so twenty per cent does not land as generous. It lands as: this one is new here.
GUIRI ALERT. George here. Two ways to get this one wrong, and each of them has a flag on it.
The American leaves twenty per cent and beams. The waiter beams back and files him, quietly, under visitor.
The Brit builds a small cairn of coppers on the saucer, apologises to it, then apologises again at the door.
Round it up, or leave nothing. Both are entirely ordinary here. The only wrong answer is a performance.
So how does it physically happen? You put the notes down and you say four words. That is the whole business.
That's fine as it is, thanks. — four words that leave the coins where they are.
It says nothing about who you are talking to, which is why it works at every counter you will stand at.

steps.promptPt: Morning coffee at the counter, one euro forty, you have put a two-euro piece down and he is turning for the till. Speak now.
steps.pt: leave the sixty where it is

steps.promptPt: The man who carried both cases up three floors is stood in your doorway, you have handed him two euros, and he is now fishing in his pocket. Speak now.
steps.pt: the same four, in a doorway
There is a second one, for an older man at a smart hotel, or a driver who has got out to lift the boot for you.
Keep the change. — a whole sentence, and there is nothing to add to it.

steps.promptPt: Eleven forty on the meter of the taxi, you have handed over twelve, and he has his hand on the little machine to give you sixty cents back. Speak now.
steps.pt: the sixty is his
One habit worth picking up before you go out: a couple of euros in coins, because little plates take coins.
👂 'Card or cash?' — asked at the till, and either answer is completely ordinary.
Cash, please. — the answer that leaves something behind on the plate.

steps.promptPt: Sunday lunch is finished, he has asked you which of the two it will be, and you already have the coins in your pocket for it. Speak now.
steps.pt: the one with coins in it
Now the job that sits outside the table. The walk finishes in a square, the guide thanks you, and steps back.
On a walk sold as free, what goes into that hand at the end is the wage. Drifting off is where this one goes wrong.
So sort it out early. You are at the counter of the bar you had a coffee in, and all you have on you is a fifty.
I'd like some change, please.
That front is the frame you have had since part twelve. Today it carries something you can put in a hand.

steps.promptPt: The walk ends in ten minutes and the only thing in your pocket is a fifty. Nobody puts a fifty in a guide's hand. Speak now.
steps.pt: what a fifty has to become
Then you go up to her, put it in her hand, and use the one you already own from part twenty-five.
Thank you, really. — the last two words are what make it land.

steps.promptPt: The group is breaking up in the square, she is being thanked by four people at once, and you have the notes folded in your palm. Speak now.
steps.pt: to her face, not to the group
And you get the ten minutes nobody else waits for. Where to eat tonight, from the woman who walks it daily.
Last one, and it is where money most nearly turns into a scene. You reach for your wallet and a hand stops yours.
👂 'This one's on me.' — said quickly, and said as a fact rather than an offer.
Do not fight it. The wrestling over the plate is the awkward part, never the paying. Four words end it.
The next one's on me. — it settles this one and it books the next coffee.

steps.promptPt: You both have your hands out over the same little plate and he has already put a note into the barman's hand. Let it go, and put a name on tomorrow. Speak now.
steps.pt: hands off, and claim tomorrow
And then you do it. It going round is the whole point of it, and getting there first is how you take your turn.

steps.promptPt: Next morning, same counter, same man, and his hand is going into his pocket again. Get in ahead of him, in two words. Speak now.
steps.pt: two words, said first
Back to that little plate on the table. The notes go down and the coins from the change stay where they are.
Nobody counts them and nobody mentions them. And the table that leaves nothing has done an ordinary thing too.
Not the walk sold as free, mind. There it is the wage, and that is the one you pay properly, in a hand.
Round it up. That is the system, all of it. You never have to work out a percentage at a table here again.
And doing sums at the table is the bit that reads as odd there. The one doing sums is the one being watched.
Count the places. The terrace. The counter. The taxi. The square at the end of the walk. Four words each time.
Nobody gave you those sentences. You put a coin down and said four words, and you never once did a sum.
You will leave what the next table leaves, without a single sum. Most visitors pay a fifth more all fortnight.
Shadowing. Out loud, underneath them, one tap of the tongue on the r. The two you will use every single day:
That's fine as it is, thanks.
All on one, please.
One more out loud, at a counter we have not stood at yet, and this time it is six in the morning.

steps.promptPt: The station bar on the last morning, a coffee and a slice of tortilla, and you have put a five down for four sixty. Speak now.
steps.pt: the forty stays there
That is it. You paid, you left what they leave, and nobody at that table noticed you doing it. Hasta luego.

aprofundar.titulo: What gets left, who pays, and the one that is really a wage (optional reading)

secoes.corpo: Coffee or a caña standing at the counter: nothing, or the loose coins out of your change. Neighbourhood bar, or a menú del día: round the total up — fifty cents, a euro. A mid-range restaurant where the evening was genuinely lovely: five to ten per cent, and it is worth knowing that most people at the tables around you leave less than that, or nothing at all. Somewhere smart: up to ten per cent, after a glance at whether 'servicio' is already on the bill. Taxi: round it up. The porter who carries your cases, or the person who cleans your room: a euro or two, in cash. One honest caveat about all of the above, and it is the reason there are no averages in this part: there is no published series for what people actually leave in Spain — no figure from the national statistics office and none from the hospitality federation. What you have here is the convergent advice of field guides, which is why it is a shape rather than a number.

exemplos.pt: ehs-TAH byehn ah-SEE — that's fine as it is, thanks. The four words, and they fit every counter
KEH-dheh-seh kon el KAHM-byoh — keep the change, for the porter or the driver who got out of the car

secoes.titulo: Why it all stays so small
secoes.corpo: The structural fact underneath the whole table is that hospitality staff in Spain are on a salary and a collective agreement. The tip is a bonus on top, not the income, and that single sentence does more work than any amount of etiquette: it means leaving nothing harms nobody and is not read as meanness. It also explains why over-tipping does not buy what an American hand expects it to buy. Nobody was waiting for it, so twenty per cent cannot read as generous — it simply reads as somebody who has not worked out where they are. If you want the arithmetic, here it is with the working shown: an average menú del día is €14.20 (Hostelería de España and Edenred, 2026). A twenty per cent reflex on that is €2.84; rounding to €15 is €0.80; the gap is about two euros a meal. Two paid meals a day for a fortnight is twenty-eight meals, so roughly €57 a head, about €115 for a couple. The British ten per cent reflex costs around €17 a head over the same trip. Treat all of that as a projection off one published average, not as a measurement — and then forget it, because the money was never the interesting part.

exemplos.pt: sohn kah-TOR-theh kon BAYN-teh — 👂 that's fourteen twenty. Two 'th' sounds and the price of lunch

secoes.titulo: Todo junto, por separado, a partes iguales — and the round that comes back to you
secoes.corpo: Three ways a bill gets settled, and the waiter will usually ask you which before he rings anything up. 'Todo junto' is all on one — you are getting this. 'Pagamos por separado' is each of us our own, and the important half of that one, from part fourteen, is that you say it before he closes anything rather than after. 'Pagamos a partes iguales' is one total divided evenly, which is the easiest of the three for him and the commonest at a table of friends. Splitting a bill item by item is friction here and generally does not happen. The other custom sitting alongside it is the round: one person settles the whole thing and the next one comes round to you. 'Invito yo' is what you will hear, said quickly and said as a fact; the honest answer is not to get your wallet out but 'la próxima invito yo', and then actually to do it the next morning. The wrestling match over the little plate is the part that turns money into a scene, and losing that wrestling match gracefully is the skill. Two places where it does not apply: somebody you have just met and will not see again, and a bill big enough to hurt — there, 'por separado', early and cheerfully.

exemplos.pt: bah TOH-dhoh KHOON-toh — 👂 all on one, or separately? The question that arrives before the bill does
lah PROHK-see-mah een-BEE-toh yoh — the next one's on me. It settles this one and books the next

secoes.titulo: Who you are talking to, and why 'está bien así' dodges the question
secoes.corpo: 'Está bien así, gracias' has a quiet virtue that is easy to miss: it contains nothing at all about the person opposite you. No tú, no usted, no decision to make while somebody is holding a card machine. That is exactly why it is the workhorse of this part and why it turns up at a bar counter, a hotel doorway and a station café without changing a syllable. 'Quédese con el cambio' does carry that decision — it is the usted shape — and we recorded it that way because the two places you are most likely to want it are an older man carrying your cases and a driver who has got out of the car to lift the boot. In a young bar, among people already on tú with you, 'quédate con el cambio' is the version flying about, and nothing breaks if you use the one you remember. If you want to sidestep the whole question, hand the money over and say the four words instead. That is what most of this part is quietly built to let you do.

exemplos.pt: KEH-dhah-teh kon el KAHM-byoh — 👂 the tú version, for a bar where you are already on first-name terms

secoes.titulo: The free tour, and the ten minutes afterwards
secoes.corpo: The walking tour advertised as free is the single role you will meet in Spain with a real expectation attached to it, and it works differently from everything else in this part: what people put into the guide's hand at the end is not a bonus on top of a wage, it is the wage. The guide has usually paid a per-head fee to the company that sent you, so a group that drifts off costs her money rather than merely disappointing her. Practicalities, in order. Get change before the walk ends — 'quería cambio, por favor' at any counter, because nobody hands over a fifty and nobody has a card machine in a square. Go up to her rather than joining the vague semicircle: a note in the hand, eye contact, 'muchas gracias, de verdad'. And then stay for the ten minutes almost nobody waits for, which is when you ask where to eat tonight and get an answer from a person who walks that street every day. That answer is routinely worth more than the walk was. A ticketed tour you booked and paid for online is a different animal entirely: it was settled at the checkout and nothing further is expected of you.

exemplos.pt: keh-REE-ah KAHM-byoh — I'd like some change, please. The opener from part twelve, doing a new job
KWAN-toh SWEH-leh dhar lah KHEN-teh — 👂 how much do people usually give? Ask another walker, not the guide
